title: Confidence in government and rumors amongst migrant worker men involved in dormitory outbreaks of COVID-19: A cross-sectional survey
screen_reason: Cross-sectional survey of 1,011 low-waged male migrant workers in Singapore that asked, for each of five named, widely-disseminated COVID-19 rumors, whether the respondent had heard, believed or shared it. The paper reports the share of respondents who had heard at least one rumor (88.9%), the share with high exposure (3-5 rumors; 53.1%) and the share who shared at least one rumor (16.4%) - self-reported exposure to and sharing of misinformation with an explicit denominator, i.e. RECALL. Belief in the rumors (54.2%) is reported too but belief is excluded by protocol.

estimates.platform: Cross-sectional survey (in-person at dormitories, transient accommodation, construction sites and a recreation centre; plus an online link advertised on posters and WhatsApp/Telegram groups); rumors could have been heard through any channel
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who had heard at least one of five widely-disseminated COVID-19 rumors
estimates.denominator: 1,011 male low-waged migrant workers in Singapore involved in dormitory COVID-19 outbreaks (COVID-19 Migrant Health Study)
estimates.definition: Respondent answered 'yes' to having HEARD at least one of five pre-specified COVID-19 rumors: drinking water frequently prevents infection; eating garlic prevents infection; the outbreak arose from people eating bat soup; the virus was created in a US lab to affect China's economy; the virus was created in a Chinese lab as a bioweapon.
estimates.misinfo_def: "To assess rumor spread, participants also indicated whether they had heard, believed, or shared each of the following COVID-19 rumors (yes / no) ... On a global scale, these rumors have been widely disseminated and have been studied in other surveys."
estimates.source_quote: Against this backdrop, 88.9% (95% CI: 86.6-90.8%) of participants had heard at least one COVID-19 rumor (mean exposure: 2.64 rumors, SD = 1.53), with the most widely-heard rumor being that drinking water frequently can prevent infection (rate of hearing: 70.5%, 95% CI: 67.6-73.3%) (Fig. 1).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Coded self_report because the instrument is the respondent's own yes/no report of having heard, believed or shared each rumor; the five rumors themselves were pre-specified by the researchers as widely disseminated false COVID-19 rumors, following analogous Ebola and COVID-19 surveys (Liu and Tong, 2020; Mesch and Schwirian, 2019) and matching the item set used by Long et al. (2021) in the Singapore resident population. No external verification of exposure, and no coder reliability applies.
estimates.moderator_quote: Data were taken from the COVID-19 Migrant Health Study, a cross-sectional survey conducted in Singapore between 22 June to 11 October 2020 (Saw et al., 2021). Respondents were male migrants employed in manual labor jobs ... Recruitment took place in-person at: (1) a dormitory complex associated with the largest COVID-19 cluster, (2) transient accommodation for workers relocated from dormitories, (3) construction work sites, and (4) a recreation center for migrant workers.
estimates.notes: population_scope coded 'other' rather than general_public: the sample is deliberately a special population (low-waged male migrant workers aged 21+, 86.9% construction sector) that the paper explicitly contrasts with the Singapore resident population. sampling_frame coded convenience: site-based in-person recruitment plus an advertised online link, no probability frame, though a 78.5% response rate is reported.

estimates.value_raw: 16.4% (95% CI: 14.2-18.9%); Table 1: 'Shared at least one rumor 166 (16.4)' of 1,011
estimates.denominator: 1,011 male low-waged migrant workers in Singapore involved in dormitory COVID-19 outbreaks

estimates.source_quote: Finally, few participants (16.4%, 95% CI: 14.2-18.9%) shared COVID-19 rumors with others (mean rumors shared = 0.27, SD = 0.74). Overall rates of rumor-sharing were similar across rumors (range: 3.7% to 7.9%)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-reported sharing of the same five researcher-specified rumors, subject to social desirability: the authors note answers "may reflect recollection biases or social pressures (e.g., fear of repercussions within a host country)". Coded self_report because the instrument is the respondent's own yes/no report of having heard, believed or shared each rumor; the five rumors themselves were pre-specified by the researchers as widely disseminated false COVID-19 rumors, following analogous Ebola and COVID-19 surveys (Liu and Tong, 2020; Mesch and Schwirian, 2019) and matching the item set used by Long et al. (2021) in the Singapore resident population. No external verification of exposure, and no coder reliability applies.

estimates.notes: Self-reported sharing, so RECALL with recall_subtype sharing rather than the behavioural SHARING construct.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Belief: '1 in 2 participants (54.2%, 95% CI: 51.1-57.3%) reported that they believed at least one COVID-19 rumor' and 'the most widely believed rumor was that drinking water was a preventive measure (rate of belief: 40.6%...)'. Belief in false claims is excluded by protocol, so no row. (2) Per-rumor hearing rates (e.g. drinking water, 70.5%, 95% CI: 67.6-73.3%) and per-rumor sharing rates ('range: 3.7% to 7.9%') are reported in Fig. 1; not extracted as separate rows because they are single-item components of the same measure in the same country x platform cell, and only the water rumor's rate is given numerically in the text (the rest are only in the figure). (3) Mean counts (mean exposure 2.64 rumors, mean believed 1.02, mean shared 0.27) are means, not shares, so no row. (4) The comparison figures for the Singapore resident population (86.2% confident; 60.9% judging infection unlikely; mean exposure 3.34, mean believed 0.27, mean shared 0.18) are taken from earlier surveys by other/overlapping teams (Liu and Tong, 2020; Long et al., 2021), i.e. figures the paper cites from elsewhere, excluded by R8. (5) Confidence in government (90.0%) and fear measures are not misinformation estimates.

rob.design: Cross-sectional survey of the COVID-19 Migrant Health Study, Singapore, 22 June - 11 October 2020; N = 1,011 male migrant workers aged 21+ holding a government-issued work permit; 78.5% response rate (87.2% in-person, 882/1011; 12.8% online, 129/1011); non-probability site-based recruitment at a dormitory complex tied to the largest cluster, transient accommodation, construction sites and a recreation centre, plus an advertised online link at quarantine sites and dormitories; instruments in English, Bengali, Tamil and Mandarin with audio and written text to accommodate low literacy; rumor items are five pre-specified yes/no claims (heard / believed / shared); analysis by counts (%) with 95% CIs and binary logistic regression with Bonferroni-corrected alpha 0.006. Limitations acknowledged: single time point and self-report subject to recall bias and social pressure. No inter-rater reliability applicable.
rob.item6_quote: To assess rumor spread, participants also indicated whether they had heard, believed, or shared each of the following COVID-19 rumors (yes / no): (1) drinking water frequently will help prevent infection (COVID-19 prevention); (2) eating garlic can help prevent infection (COVID-19 prevention); (3) the outbreak arose from people eating bat soup (COVID-19 origins); (4) the virus was created in a US lab to affect China's economy (COVID-19 origins); and (5) the virus was created in a Chinese lab as a bioweapon (COVID-19 origins).
